request: We need an app for staff to check attendees in at the venue entrance on the event day.

problem.value: Ensure attendees are identified and let in efficiently at the entrance; underlying driver (speed, security, headcount, billing) unclear
problem.evidence: "check attendees in at the venue entrance" gives the action but not the reason behind it

current_process.evidence: not mentioned — paper list, spreadsheet, or nothing yet?

actors.value: Staff operate the check-in at the door; attendees are the subject
actors.evidence: "staff to check attendees in" — event manager, security, exhibitor not mentioned

business_objects.value: Attendee, Event, Check-in; Registration/Category source unspecified
business_objects.evidence: implies an attendee list exists but its origin isn't stated

business_rules.evidence: no rule on duplicates, re-entry, category-based access

workflow.value: Identify attendee → mark as arrived; multi-zone/session/re-entry lifecycle unclear
workflow.evidence: context flags check-in as routinely multi-meaning, unaddressed in request

integrations.evidence: no mention of offline mode, sync with registration system, or notifications

questions.q: Will the check-in app need to work when the venue's wifi/4G is unreliable — i.e. does staff need to keep checking people in even if the connection drops, with the data syncing once it's back?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: connectivity is almost never stated but decides the entire architecture (offline snapshot + sync vs. always-online); getting this wrong is the single most common cause of a failed check-in app on the day

questions.q: Where does the attendee list come from — is it imported from a registration system before the event, and can staff add someone on the spot (walk-in, substitution, name correction) at the door?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: the request only covers the check-in action, not the upstream source of the list; an assumed 'frozen import' silently breaks on walk-ins and substitutions, which are routine

questions.q: Is this a one-off build for this single event, or should it be reusable/configurable for future events (multiple events, branding, zones per event)?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: this single answer changes the data model, configurability and cost of nearly everything else in the build

questions.q: If the same attendee is scanned twice — at the same door or two different doors within seconds — what should happen: block it as a duplicate, treat it as a re-entry, or record it separately for a different zone/session?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: check-in is not a boolean; this is the classic ambiguity that changes the data model and must be decided before build, not discovered during testing

questions.q: After the event, what attendance data do you need back — who actually came, at what time, at which entrance/zone — and in what format (dashboard, export, report)?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: attendance data is typically the actual deliverable clients care about post-event, yet it's entirely unaddressed in the request

questions.q: Roughly how many attendees and how tight is the arrival window (e.g. most of the crowd in 20 minutes before a keynote)? This drives how fast each check-in needs to be.
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: throughput at the door is a functional requirement, not a nice-to-have, and a slow flow is a different product than a fast one

summary.objective: Give on-site staff a way to check attendees in at the venue entrance on the day of the event.
summary.scope: Likely includes: a staff-facing check-in interface (scan and/or manual search), a way to mark an attendee as arrived, and probably some visibility of attendance during/after the event. The exact scope — offline capability, source of the attendee list, duplicate/re-entry handling, and whether this is reusable across events — is currently undefined.
assumptions: The app must handle a fixed, non-movable event date with no possibility of post-launch fixes on the day
An attendee list exists somewhere and needs to be identified against it at the door
Staff are likely non-technical, first-time users of the tool
Some form of post-event attendance data will be expected even though not requested explicitly
summary.blind_spot: The request describes only the on-the-day action ('check attendees in') without addressing the two things that most often blow up an event check-in build: whether the app must work offline (venue connectivity is rarely reliable and is almost never mentioned by the client), and where the attendee list comes from / how it's kept current (walk-ins, substitutions, late changes). Both are architecture decisions, not settings, and are far more expensive to retrofit than to decide up front.

summary.objective: Give on-site staff a way to check attendees in at the venue entrance on the event day, producing a reliable arrival record.

Scope could expand significantly depending on connectivity, list volatility, and whether multiple zones/sessions are in play.
assumptions: A single entrance / single check-in event is assumed for now (no zones or sessions mentioned).
Staff are the sole operators, using devices provided for the day.
The event has a fixed, non-negotiable date.

briefs.problem: Staff need to reliably identify and admit attendees at the door on a fixed, unmovable date, but the request only names the action — not the connectivity, list-freshness, or check-in semantics decisions that actually determine whether the build works on the day.
briefs.solution: A staff-facing check-in app (scan plus manual search) that marks attendees as arrived and gives some visibility into attendance during and after the event.
introduces: an offline-capable local snapshot with a later sync/conflict-resolution layer
concurrency handling across multiple simultaneous entrance devices
a non-boolean check-in model distinguishing duplicate, re-entry and multi-zone access
an on-site attendee-list editing path (walk-ins, substitutions, corrections)
an event-configurability layer if this is meant to be reused across future events

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed, not confirmed
challenges.premise: The request describes 'staff scan attendees at the entrance' as if the app will simply be online.
challenges.alternative: Design for offline-first: a local snapshot of the attendee list on each device, with check-ins syncing once connectivity returns and a defined conflict-resolution rule for near-simultaneous scans.
challenges.consequence: If built online-only and the venue's wifi/4G saturates during the peak arrival window (the most likely failure point per this kind of build), check-in stalls in front of the client with no fallback.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm offline requirements and venue connectivity before locking the architecture — this decision cannot be retrofitted after build starts.

challenges.headline: One-off build vs reusable kit
challenges.premise: The request implicitly treats this as a single-event build.
challenges.alternative: Decide upfront whether this is the first instance of a reusable event kit; a multi-event data model (events, zones, categories as configurable entities) is a different shape than a single-event one, and quietly retrofitting reusability later means rebuilding the core model.
challenges.consequence: If a second event follows and the data model wasn't designed for it, the team ends up rebuilding rather than reconfiguring — at a much higher cost than deciding now.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether more events are planned before scoping or estimating.

challenges.headline: Check-in treated as a boolean
challenges.premise: 'Check attendees in' reads as a single mark-arrived action.
challenges.alternative: Model check-in as a typed event (first entry, re-entry, zone/session-specific access) so a second scan of the same attendee has a defined, deliberate outcome rather than an accidental one.
challenges.consequence: A naive boolean model breaks the first time someone re-enters after stepping out, or a second door scans them within seconds — exactly the scenario that surfaces during rehearsal or, worse, live at the door.
challenges.recommendation: Define duplicate vs re-entry vs zone-access semantics with the client before building the data model.

decisions.decision: Staff will use a dedicated interface supporting both badge/QR scanning and manual name search
decisions.why: Scanning alone fails routinely in real conditions — dim screens, crumpled printouts, misspelled names — and a manual fallback is needed for every arrival, not just edge cases.
decisions.tradeoff: Extra build effort for a manual-search and on-the-spot registration path, in exchange for not stalling the line when scanning fails.

decisions.decision: The event date is treated as a hard, immovable deadline requiring an on-site rehearsal before go-live
decisions.why: There is no post-launch fix window; failure is visible immediately as a queue at the door.
decisions.alternative: Ship and iterate as with a normal software release.
decisions.tradeoff: Additional rehearsal time and cost accepted to avoid an unrecoverable failure on the day.

challenges.headline: Continuous connectivity assumed
challenges.premise: The request implicitly assumes staff devices will have reliable network access at the venue entrance.
challenges.alternative: Build offline-first: a local snapshot of the attendee list on the device, with check-ins synced later and conflicts resolved when connectivity returns.
challenges.consequence: If the venue's network is weak (basements, thick walls, saturated wifi are common), an online-only build stalls the line at the door in front of the client — the one failure mode this app cannot afford.
challenges.recommendation: Settle offline vs. online-only as an architecture decision before estimating, not as a setting to configure later.

challenges.headline: One-off build vs. reusable kit
challenges.premise: The request is framed as a single-event feature with no mention of future events.
challenges.alternative: If more events are planned, invest now in a configurable multi-event model (branding, zones, categories) instead of hardcoding this event's specifics.
challenges.consequence: Building single-event-only now and needing reuse later means redoing the configuration and data model from scratch, at a higher cost than deciding upfront.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether this is the first of a series before committing to the data model.

challenges.headline: Second scan meaning undefined
challenges.premise: The request treats 'check in' as a single, self-evident action.
challenges.alternative: Model check-in as an event log that distinguishes a duplicate (block), a re-entry after stepping out (allow), and access to a different zone or session (record separately) — real arrivals produce all three.
challenges.consequence: A naive boolean check-in breaks the moment there's a re-entry or a second zone, and concurrent scans at different doors will silently create duplicates with no defined outcome.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client what a second scan should mean before defining the data model or the workflow.

challenges.headline: Single-entrance, single-scan assumption
challenges.premise: The workflow is modeled as one scan at one entrance marking the attendee arrived, with no zones, sessions, or re-entry.
challenges.alternative: Modeling check-in as an event tied to a zone/session from day one — even with only one entrance active now — costs little extra and avoids a rebuild if the client later needs exhibitor areas, breakout rooms, or a keynote with separate access.
challenges.consequence: If zones or re-entry appear after the data model is built around a boolean 'arrived' flag, the fix touches the schema, the UI and the sync logic all at once, days before a fixed date that cannot move.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether there are, or will ever be, multiple access points, sessions, or re-entry scenarios, even for this single event.

challenges.headline: Connectivity assumed, not confirmed
challenges.premise: The request describes scanning at the venue entrance without addressing whether the devices will have reliable network access.
challenges.alternative: Designing offline-first — a local snapshot of the attendee list with check-ins queued and synced later — costs more up front but is the only version of this app that survives a venue with weak signal, which is the norm rather than the exception for this kind of build.
challenges.consequence: Building online-only and discovering a dead zone at the actual door means the check-in path — the one thing that must not fail — fails in front of the client with no time left to fix it.
challenges.recommendation: Treat a venue connectivity check as part of scoping, not an afterthought, and commit to offline-first unless the venue is proven reliable.

challenges.recommendation: Settle one-off vs. reusable kit with the client before any architecture or estimate is finalized.
